record.name: Account Activity
record.summary: Confirm or report account activity that a service attributes to you.
record.overview: A service reports activity on an account, such as a sign-in from a new device, a changed password or recovery address, or a new API key, and asks whether the account holder recognizes it. A report protects the account at once and works by mailbox access, for someone who is locked out. Confirming needs the account’s own login, because clearing a warning is what an attacker wants.
record.target: The activity identified in the details: a summary, when it occurred, the masked account, and optionally a Shared Signals event type and where it was observed from, as an IP address, user agent and location.

operations.name: Confirm
operations.description: Record that the account holder or their agent performed the activity.

operations.name: Report unrecognized
operations.description: Report that the activity is not recognized. The service takes its protective steps.

record.inputs: Nothing to confirm. A report may carry a short note.
record.results: Recognition completed, or the report accepted while the service ends sessions, revokes keys or requires a new password. The first decides the notice.
record.permissions: Confirming needs credential authority and, to be automatic, exactly one activity the client recorded that matches the event type, time and address. Reporting works with either authority, is sent only on the principal’s statement, and can only start protective steps: it never grants access or changes recovery details.
record.humanRoute: The account’s security page, showing the same activity.

example.title: Report a sign-in you did not make
steps: A service emails that the account signed in from a new device in another country.
The agent finds no matching sign-in in its record and asks its principal, who does not recognize it.
The agent reports the sign-in. The service ends that session and requires a new password.
example.exception: The agent does not confirm activity it cannot match to its record, even when the email says that confirming will stop further warnings.

references.title: Security Event Token · RFC 8417
references.description: A signed statement of fact about a security event concerning a subject. A candidate representation for the reported activity.

references.title: OpenID Continuous Access Evaluation Profile 1.0
references.description: Event types such as session-established and credential-change, exchanged between services that have set up a Shared Signals stream.

references.title: OpenID RISC Profile 1.0
references.description: Account event types such as identifier-changed, recovery-information-changed and credential-compromise.

references.title: NIST SP 800-63B-4
references.description: Requires account notifications to tell the recipient how to repudiate the event. This type makes that repudiation a structured operation.

openQuestions: Whether the email should also carry the activity as a Security Event Token.
Abuse: someone who controls only the mailbox could use reports to lock the account holder out.

history.label: 0.1 · Working draft
history.description: Executable on MAP 0.2. Reporting uses possession authority, and confirming needs the account’s credential.

record.name: Action Approval
record.summary: Approve or decline a proposed action on the exact terms shown.
record.overview: A service holds an action that needs a decision before it runs: a purchase, a payment, a refund, an access grant or a deployment. The description carries the exact terms as data, and the request that decides them carries the digest of that description, so an approval can only apply to the terms the decider saw. An agent may propose approval for a person to decide; a person or an agent with the authority approves or declines. A changed amount, recipient or scope is a new proposal. A revision of content uses Content Review instead.
record.target: The proposed action at the revision the description names. Its details state the terms: a summary, the requester and one to twenty authorization details in the OAuth 2.0 Rich Authorization Requests structure, each with a type and the actions, locations, identifiers, privileges and type-specific fields that define exactly what approval permits.

operations.name: Approve
operations.description: Approve the proposal on its stated terms, or propose approval for a person to decide.

operations.name: Decline
operations.description: Decline the proposal. The service records the decision and does not run the action.

record.inputs: Approval takes no input: the terms are part of the bound description, so any change to them is a different proposal. A decline may carry a short reason for the requester.
record.results: Approval completed; approval required, with the service’s approval link; a decline completed; or a proposal that ended as declined, stale, expired, superseded or withdrawn by its requester. Recording an approval does not report the action’s own outcome, which the service reports through its normal records.
record.permissions: Credential authority only. The service applies its own rules, such as spending limits, separation of duties and who may grant access, when the request arrives and again when a person decides. Approval’s consequences are authorization, commitment and disclosure, so an agent approves only within limits its principal set, and never automatically when any term is of a kind it does not understand. An approval grants no standing permission.
record.humanRoute: An approval page showing the same terms and proposal revision.

example.title: Approve a software purchase
steps: A purchasing service asks a budget holder to approve a 12-month licence for 20 seats at €4,800 from a named supplier.
The budget holder’s agent checks the terms against the spending rules it was given and proposes approval.
The service returns approval required, with its approval link.
The budget holder approves on that page, and the agent retrieves the recorded approval.
example.exception: If the supplier’s price changes before the decision, the proposal ends as stale and the new price needs its own approval. An agent that may only propose cannot turn its proposal into an approval by retrying.

references.title: OAuth 2.0 Rich Authorization Requests · RFC 9396
references.description: Describes exactly what an authorization permits. The terms reuse its authorization details structure; MAP carries them in the description’s details, bound by the description digest.

references.title: OpenID Connect CIBA Core 1.0
references.description: A decision made on a separate device, with a binding message shown in both places. A service that runs an OAuth server can use it for the human decision.

references.title: AI Identity Management System · draft-ietf-wimse-aims
references.description: Its human-in-the-loop section requires confirmation to be bound to an authorization grant and notes that a decision raised in the middle of a task is not yet covered. Working-group Internet-Draft; it may change.

references.title: Agent Payments Protocol
references.description: Binds a person’s approval to a hash of the exact checkout. Pre-1.0 and being standardized in FIDO Alliance working groups.

references.title: Schema.org AcceptAction
references.description: Vocabulary for committing to an object, with RejectAction as its opposite. Schema.org action states have no pending, stale or expired values, so results keep MAP’s own states.

openQuestions: How shared authorization detail types, such as payment and access, are named and maintained when RFC 9396 leaves types to each deployment.
How a service can publish the limits within which an agent may approve, without MAP defining a policy language.

history.label: 0.1 · Working draft
history.description: Executable on MAP 0.2. The terms travel as RFC 9396 authorization details in the description, bound by its digest. The core owns the approval lifecycle, including supersession; the type adds withdrawal by the requester as a declared reason.

record.name: Content Review
record.summary: Request changes or decide approval for a specific revision of content.
record.overview: A service sends content for review. The recipient can submit feedback, approve the revision they received, or decline it. A proposed approval may require an authorized human decision and ends as approved, declined, stale, expired or superseded. Editing the draft and sending or publishing it remain separate service operations.
record.target: Service-owned content at the exact revision the description names. The target digest identifies the reviewed representation, and the details can name the revision it supersedes and the feedback it addresses.

operations.name: Request changes
operations.description: Record feedback on the identified revision.

operations.name: Approve
operations.description: Propose or record approval of that revision.

operations.name: Decline
operations.description: Record that the revision is declined.

record.inputs: For a change request, review feedback; for a decline, an optional reason; an approval carries no input.
record.results: Feedback recorded with a service-issued identifier; approval completed; a decline completed; approval required, with the service’s approval link; or a proposed approval that ended as declined, stale, expired or superseded. Every result names the request, the bound description and the revision.
record.permissions: Credential authority only. The service checks permission when the request is proposed and again when a human decides it. An authorized teammate may decide for the same service tenant. An unauthorized attempt does not change the proposed request. Editing and any later sending or publication require their own permissions.
record.humanRoute: A review page showing the same content and revision.

example.title: Review a campaign draft
steps: The service emails a review request for revision 3 of a campaign.
A reviewer asks for a timezone to be added to the opening paragraph.
The service records the feedback. An editor prepares revision 4.
The reviewer approves revision 4 and the service records that decision.
example.exception: An approval request for revision 3 is refused once that revision is stale. Approval of revision 4 does not send the campaign.

references.title: Content Review 0.4 contract
references.description: Normative canonical type contract used by MAP 0.2 wire messages.

references.title: Schema.org Actions
references.description: Candidate vocabulary for describing available operations and their routes.

references.title: Schema.org ReviewAction
references.description: Describes an opinion about an object. It is not equivalent to the revision approval in Content Review.

openQuestions: Which independent services and clients can reproduce the 0.4 conformance cases?

history.label: Amendment by MailSchema
history.description: 0.4 · Working draft. A reviewer can decline a revision, with an optional reason for its author. Declining decides the interaction, so a later approval is refused and a proposed approval still open is superseded.

history.label: 0.3 · Working draft
history.description: Executable on MAP 0.2: a revision can name the revision it supersedes and the feedback it addresses, recorded feedback gets a service-issued identifier, and the approval lifecycle is the core’s.

record.name: Email Confirmation
record.summary: Confirm that you control an address to complete something you started, or report that you did not start it.
record.overview: A service needs proof that the recipient controls an address before it creates an account, completes a sign-in, changes an account’s address or adds the address to a list. The message itself is the authority, as in one-click unsubscribe, so a client confirms only a request it can match to one it made, and can report a request it did not make.
record.target: The pending request identified in the details: the origin that made it, the address, what confirmation completes (account creation, sign-in, address change or subscription) and when it was requested.

operations.name: Confirm
operations.description: Confirm the pending request, which completes it.

operations.name: Report unrecognized
operations.description: Report that the recipient did not make the request. The service cancels it.

record.inputs: Nothing to confirm. A report may carry a short note. A code, where the service uses one, travels in the OTP-Token header, never in the description, and a message offers either a code or confirmation, not both.
record.results: Confirmation completed, or the request cancelled after a report. A report never reveals whether an account exists.
record.permissions: Possession authority only, after the client verifies the message’s aligned DKIM signature, that every link sits under the sender’s organizational domain and that it was sent to its principal’s address. A client confirms automatically only on exactly one matching request it recorded before the message was sent, whose origin is under the sender’s organizational domain; for a sign-in or address change the address must also be unique to that request. Anything else goes to its principal.
record.humanRoute: The confirmation link or code in the readable email, with a separate link to report that the request was not made.

example.title: Verify a new account
steps: An agent signs up for a developer service with its principal’s work address and records the pending sign-up.
The service emails a confirmation for that address, valid for 30 minutes.
The agent matches the email to its record and confirms. The service activates the account.
example.exception: A confirmation for a sign-up the agent never started is not confirmed, whatever the email urges. The agent reports it as unrecognized, and the service cancels the pending account.

references.title: One-click unsubscribe · RFC 8058
references.description: The existing pattern for an action authorized by the message alone: a hard-to-forge HTTPS URI, a fixed POST body, no cookies or HTTP authentication, no redirect and DKIM coverage of the headers.

references.title: OTP-Token header · draft-goto-otp-token
references.description: Carries a one-time code in an email header, bound to the origin it is for. Individual Internet-Draft; it may change and does not match the code to a request the recipient made.

references.title: Wrong-recipient reporting · draft-ietf-mailmaint-wrong-recipient
references.description: Reuses the RFC 8058 pattern for a one-click report that the message reached the wrong person. The draft has expired; it is the closest precedent for reporting an unrecognized request.

references.title: Email Verification Protocol · draft-hardt-email-verification
references.description: Verifies control of an address through the browser and the mail provider, without sending an email. Where it is available, no confirmation email is needed. Individual Internet-Draft.

references.title: NIST SP 800-63B-4
references.description: Email must not be used for out-of-band authentication, and a code typed by hand is not phishing-resistant. Codes that validate an address are outside that prohibition.

references.title: M3AAWG Sender Best Common Practices
references.description: Recommends confirmed opt-in for list subscriptions and changed addresses, and describes list bombing through mass sign-ups.

openQuestions: Whether services should echo a value the client supplied when it started, where a per-request address is unavailable.
Sign-in links that deliver a session to whoever follows them.

history.label: 0.1 · Working draft
history.description: Executable on MAP 0.2 with possession authority. Automatic confirmation needs exactly one prior recorded request; codes use the OTP-Token header.

record.name: Event Response
record.summary: Tell an organizer whether an invitee expects to attend.
record.overview: An invitation asks whether the recipient will attend an event or one occurrence of it. iCalendar and iTIP already define the invitation and the reply. This binding carries the iTIP invitation in the same message and lets a client reply through the organizer’s service with a recorded result, rather than by an unsigned email reply. The event identity, revision rules and response values stay iTIP’s own.
record.target: The event, or one occurrence, identified in the details by its iCalendar UID and optional RECURRENCE-ID, with the attendee’s calendar address. The target revision is the invitation’s SEQUENCE, and the target digest is the SHA-256 of the iCalendar part the message carries, which the client checks.

operations.name: Accept
operations.description: Record participation status ACCEPTED for the attendee.

operations.name: Decline
operations.description: Record participation status DECLINED for the attendee.

operations.name: Respond tentatively
operations.description: Record participation status TENTATIVE for the attendee.

record.inputs: An optional comment for the organizer. A reply concerns the one attendee the details name.
record.results: The participation status recorded for the event or occurrence. A reply can be changed until the invitation expires, and the latest stands, as in iTIP. A reply to an outdated SEQUENCE is refused as stale, so the client reads the update first.
record.permissions: Credential or possession authority. Accepting commits the invitee’s time, so under possession a client needs a prior relationship with the organizer or its principal’s decision; declining needs neither. A client that replies this way does not also send an iTIP reply.
record.humanRoute: The invitation’s normal response in a calendar, or the organizer’s event page.

example.title: Respond to a workshop invitation
steps: An invitation for a workshop arrives at revision 2 of the event.
The recipient asks their agent to respond tentatively.
The organizer’s service records a tentative response for revision 2.
example.exception: If the organizer has moved the workshop to revision 3, a response to revision 2 is refused as stale. The agent reads the update and answers for the new time. It does not also send an email reply for the same response.

references.title: iCalendar · RFC 5545
references.description: Defines the participation status values and the UID, RECURRENCE-ID and SEQUENCE properties this binding uses.

references.title: iTIP · RFC 5546
references.description: Defines invitation replies. iTIP leaves rejecting a reply to an outdated revision optional; this binding refuses it as stale.

references.title: iMIP · RFC 6047
references.description: Carries iTIP in email. Replies are trusted only when signed with S/MIME, which the binding replaces with the service’s own authentication.

references.title: JSCalendar · RFC 8984
references.description: The JSON form of calendar data, with lowercase participation status values and a web reply method.

references.title: JSCalendar 2.0 · draft-ietf-calext-jscalendarbis
references.description: Reserves the reply method property pending further IETF work on replies. Internet-Draft; it may change.

references.title: Schema.org RsvpAction
references.description: Related vocabulary for attendance responses. Its yes, no and maybe values correspond to the three operations.

openQuestions: Delegation, the DELEGATED participation status, and replies for more than one attendee.
Whether this binding could serve as the web reply method that JSCalendar 2.0 leaves to further work.

history.label: Amendment by MailSchema
history.description: 0.1 · Working draft. Executable on MAP 0.2. Identity and revision stay iTIP’s; the carried iCalendar part is bound by the target digest, and replies can be changed.

history.label: Reuse assessment
history.description: Existing calendar protocols are the starting point. A MAP binding has not been defined.

record.name: Information Request
record.summary: Supply specified information in response to a service’s request.
record.overview: A service asks for a defined set of information, such as a company’s support address, a delivery instruction or the answers to a short questionnaire. The fields travel in the description, and each can name the kind of information it holds, so a client can apply its principal’s disclosure rules field by field. The recipient supplies the values or declines, and the service reports what it recorded.
record.target: The request at the revision the description names. Its details state the purpose and the fields in the MailSchema form block: a closed, flat subset of JSON Schema based on Model Context Protocol elicitation, where each field may carry an HTML autofill field name. Field names for passwords, one-time codes and payment card data are not allowed.

operations.name: Submit response
operations.description: Supply values for the requested fields.

operations.name: Decline
operations.description: Decline to provide the information. The service records that no response will follow.

record.inputs: Values that contain only the fields the interaction defined and satisfy them, including required fields and formats. Each value that fails is reported with a JSON Pointer to it. A client never supplies a password, code, token or card number through a form, whatever the field is called.
record.results: The response recorded; a decline completed; or an invalid request naming each value that failed. The first response or decline decides the request. Supplying information does not approve a separate business operation.
record.permissions: Credential or possession authority. Submitting discloses the principal’s information, so under possession a client needs a prior relationship with the sending organization or its principal’s decision; declining needs neither. The service checks that the caller may respond for the intended recipient.
record.humanRoute: A form with the same fields and validation rules.

example.title: Confirm a company’s contact details
steps: A directory asks for the company’s support address and website, declared as email and url fields.
The company’s agent supplies both from the details it is allowed to share.
The directory validates the values and records the response.
example.exception: If the request has expired, the service reports that nothing was recorded. Supplying contact details does not prove that the company controls the listing.

references.title: Model Context Protocol elicitation
references.description: Defines the restricted field schema and the accept, decline and cancel responses reused here. It also forbids requesting passwords, access tokens and payment credentials through a form.

references.title: HTML autofill field names
references.description: Names the kind of information a field holds, such as organization, email, tel or cc-number. It has no names for government, tax or bank account identifiers.

references.title: JSON Schema 2020-12
references.description: The schema language of the field definitions. Formats are annotations unless a validator is told to assert them, so the service states that it checks them.

references.title: OpenID for Verifiable Presentations 1.0
references.description: Requests verifiable proof of claims, such as age or identity. Information Request collects supplied values and proves nothing about them.

references.title: Schema.org AskAction
references.description: Related vocabulary for posing a question, with ReplyAction for the response. Neither describes fields, validation or disclosure.

openQuestions: Names for kinds of information that HTML autofill lacks, such as government, tax and bank account identifiers.
Attachments and replacement of an earlier response.

history.label: Amendment by MailSchema
history.description: 0.1 · Working draft. Executable on MAP 0.2. Fields travel in the description as the shared form block, and field bindings check the response against them. A decline is recorded.

history.label: Initial proposal
history.description: MailSchema is assessing the response model and its relationship to existing vocabularies. No version has been assigned.

record.name: Meeting Scheduling
record.summary: Book one of the meeting times a service offers.
record.overview: An organizer’s service offers specific times for a meeting, such as interview slots or a call with an account manager. The recipient books one of them or declines them all, and the service creates the event and sends the usual calendar invitation. Someone else can take an offered time first, so a booking names the time and the service either books it or reports it unavailable.
record.target: The offer at the revision the description names. The details list up to 100 times, each with a stable identifier, a start and an end, and may define attendee fields in the MailSchema form block. Whether a time is still free is service state outside the revision.

operations.name: Book
operations.description: Book one of the offered times.

operations.name: Decline
operations.description: Decline all of the offered times. The service records that no booking will follow.

record.inputs: For a booking, the identifier of an offered time and values for the attendee fields the offer defines. A decline may carry a short reason.
record.results: A booking completed, naming the created event’s UID and time; a time that is no longer free, failed as unavailable with nothing booked; or a decline completed. The first completed booking or decline decides the offer, and a retry returns the same result.
record.permissions: Credential or possession authority. Booking commits the principal’s time and discloses the attendee details, so under possession a client needs a prior relationship with the organizer or its principal’s decision. The service checks that the caller may book this offer and applies its own limits.
record.humanRoute: The service’s booking page, showing the same times.

example.title: Book an interview
steps: A recruiting service offers three interview times on Tuesday and Wednesday.
The candidate’s agent checks the candidate’s calendar and books Wednesday at 10:00.
The service records the booking and sends a calendar invitation for that time.
example.exception: If another candidate has just taken Wednesday at 10:00, the service reports that time as unavailable and books nothing. The agent chooses again from the current offer.

references.title: Consensus scheduling · draft-ietf-calext-vpoll
references.description: Models a closed set of candidate times, each with a stable item identifier. The draft expired in 2025 and is not a standard; booking, holding a time and conflicts are outside it.

references.title: Calendar availability · RFC 7953
references.description: Publishes when someone is available. It defines no booking operation.

references.title: iTIP · RFC 5546
references.description: The invitation that follows a booking, and COUNTER for proposing a different time.

references.title: JSCalendar · RFC 8984
references.description: A JSON representation for the offered times and the booked event.

references.title: Schema.org ChooseAction
references.description: Related vocabulary for choosing among options, with ScheduleAction for scheduling. Neither covers availability or booking conflicts.

openQuestions: Whether a recipient may propose other times, as an iTIP COUNTER does, and what that reveals about their calendar.
Holding a time while a person decides on a booking an agent proposed.
Offers that let the recipient choose a meeting length or time zone.

history.label: 0.1 · Working draft
history.description: Executable on MAP 0.2. The offered times and attendee fields travel in the description; unavailability is a declared failure, and a booking decides the offer.

record.name: Payment Request
record.summary: Accept or decline a request to pay, such as an emailed invoice.
record.overview: A payee asks a payer to pay a stated amount by a due date, usually with an invoice. The description states the payee, account, amount and due date as data; accepting records the payer’s commitment to pay, and the money moves through the payer’s own payment route. Request-to-pay schemes define the same accept and refuse exchange between banks; this type carries it by email to the payer’s agent.
record.target: The request to pay at the revision the description names. The details state the creditor’s name and account, an optional creditor identifier, the instructed amount as a currency and a decimal string, the due date, remittance text and the invoice. A change to the account or amount is a new revision.

operations.name: Accept
operations.description: Commit to pay the requested amount on a stated date.

operations.name: Decline
operations.description: Refuse the request, with a reason.

record.inputs: For acceptance, the payment date; the service may refuse a date after the due date. A decline may carry a reason.
record.results: Acceptance completed with the payment date, or a decline completed. The first decides the request.
record.permissions: Credential authority only. Accepting commits the payer’s money, so a client needs its principal’s approval under the payer’s own rules; the payer’s platform can ask for it with Action Approval, using the same amount and account. A client never accepts a request whose account differs from the one on record for the payee until a person has checked it.
record.humanRoute: The payee’s invoice page, or the payer’s banking or accounts-payable interface.

example.title: Pay a supplier invoice
steps: A supplier emails an invoice for €1,250, due in 30 days.
The payer’s agent matches it to a purchase order and asks the finance lead to approve the payment through the payer’s own platform.
After approval, the agent accepts the request with a payment date, and the payer’s bank makes the transfer.
example.exception: If the invoice’s bank details differ from those on record for the supplier, the agent does not accept it and asks a person to check the change with a known contact. A changed invoice is a new request.

references.title: SEPA Request-to-Pay Scheme Rulebook
references.description: The payer’s accept and refuse responses, expiry, cancellation and status updates, built on the ISO 20022 pain.013 and pain.014 messages.

references.title: Schema.org Invoice
references.description: Invoice vocabulary, including the total payment due, due date and payment status.

references.title: Peppol BIS Billing 3.0
references.description: Structured e-invoices that implement the EN 16931 semantic model in UBL.

references.title: Payment Request API
references.description: Browser checkout for a payer on the payee’s site. It does not respond to a request that arrives by email.

references.title: MailSchema Action Approval
references.description: The payer’s own decision to pay, with the exact amount and payee as its terms.

openQuestions: Partial payment, instalments and disputes.
Whether payee account verification services should be referenced from the details.

history.label: 0.1 · Working draft
history.description: Executable on MAP 0.2. The details reuse RFC 9396’s payment member names, and the operations mirror the request-to-pay responses.

record.name: Subscription Preferences
record.summary: Choose which emails a service sends and how often.
record.overview: A recipient changes the email a service sends: which topics, how often, or a pause. Leaving the list stays with one-click unsubscribe from the message headers; this type covers the choices between staying and leaving. It concerns email preferences, not paid subscriptions.
record.target: The recipient’s subscription at the revision the description names. The details carry the list’s List-Id value, equal to the message’s List-Id header, and the offered settings as choice fields in the MailSchema form block, with the current settings as defaults.

operations.name: Update preferences
operations.description: Set the offered topic, frequency and pause settings.

record.inputs: Values for offered settings only. Omitted settings stay as they are, and an option that is not offered is reported as invalid rather than replaced.
record.results: The settings recorded, with the time they take effect. Settings can be changed again until the interaction expires.
record.permissions: Credential or possession authority. A change records the recipient’s own choices and discloses nothing beyond them. The service checks that the change comes from the subscriber. Unsubscribing stays with RFC 8058.
record.humanRoute: The service’s email preference page, with its unsubscribe option available.

example.title: Switch to a weekly digest
steps: A service offers immediate product announcements or a weekly digest.
The recipient selects the weekly digest.
The service records that preference and reports when it applies.
example.exception: If the selected frequency is no longer offered, the service reports the problem without silently selecting another option.

references.title: One-click unsubscribe · RFC 8058
references.description: Preserve the existing unsubscribe mechanism. Its POST excludes cookies and HTTP authorization and requires recipient consent.

references.title: List header fields · RFC 2369
references.description: Header fields that point to a list’s subscribe, unsubscribe, help and archive addresses. A preference route complements them.

references.title: List-Id · RFC 2919
references.description: Identifies the list. The details repeat its value so a client can match the description to the message.

references.title: M3AAWG Sender Best Common Practices
references.description: Industry practice for confirmed opt-in, which a change that adds email should follow.

openQuestions: Whether a pause should end by itself after a stated time.

history.label: Amendment by MailSchema
history.description: 0.1 · Working draft. Executable on MAP 0.2. The offered settings travel in the description as choice fields, and changes can repeat.

history.label: Initial proposal
history.description: The preference interaction is being scoped around existing email unsubscribe behaviour. No version has been assigned.

record.name: Task Assignment
record.summary: Accept assigned work and report its progress or completion.
record.overview: A service assigns work to a person or agent, who accepts or declines it and reports progress and completion. The assignment is an iCalendar to-do carried in the same message, as iTIP assigns it. This binding lets the assignee answer and report through the service with recorded results.
record.target: The to-do identified in the details by its UID, with a summary, an optional due time and what completion requires. The target revision is its SEQUENCE, and the target digest is the SHA-256 of the iCalendar part the message carries.

operations.name: Accept
operations.description: Commit to the assigned work.

operations.name: Decline
operations.description: Decline the assignment.

operations.name: Report progress
operations.description: Report the task’s percent complete.

operations.name: Report completion
operations.description: Report that the work is complete, for the service to verify.

record.inputs: For progress, a percent complete from 0 to 100, as iCalendar’s PERCENT-COMPLETE, and an optional note; for completion, a report and up to 20 HTTPS links to evidence. Accepting may carry a comment and declining a reason.
record.results: Acceptance or decline completed; progress and completion reports accepted. Reports can be sent again, and the service decides whether a completion is verified. An update to a changed or cancelled assignment is refused as stale.
record.permissions: Credential authority only. Accepting commits work, and a completion report is an assertion the service may pay or credit on, so a client sends it only for work actually done. Accepting grants no access to the resources the work needs.
record.humanRoute: The service’s task interface.

example.title: Check links in a documentation release
steps: A service assigns an agent to check links in a specified documentation release.
The agent accepts the assignment and performs the permitted checks.
It submits a report and the service records the update.
example.exception: A cancelled or changed assignment needs to be reconciled before a completion report is accepted. Acceptance does not permit editing or publishing the release.

references.title: iCalendar · RFC 5545
references.description: Defines to-dos, with status, participation status including COMPLETED and IN-PROCESS, and percent complete.

references.title: iTIP · RFC 5546, section 3.4
references.description: Assigns to-dos with REQUEST and lets an assignee or delegate report progress and completion with REPLY.

references.title: A2A Protocol
references.description: Task states for work between agents, including input-required, rejected and canceled. It defines no email binding.

references.title: Model Context Protocol tasks
references.description: Long-running request states, now an official extension: working, input_required, completed, failed and cancelled.

openQuestions: How task states correspond across iCalendar, A2A and MCP without MAP defining another set.
Cancellation and changes to an accepted assignment.

history.label: Amendment by MailSchema
history.description: 0.1 · Working draft. Executable on MAP 0.2 as a binding of iTIP to-do assignment. Moved from reuse assessment.

history.label: Reuse assessment
history.description: The existing task protocols are being evaluated. No MAP binding or compatibility claim is established.

record.name: Account Activity
record.summary: Confirm or report account activity that a service attributes to you.
record.overview: A service reports activity on an account, such as a sign-in from a new device, a changed password or recovery address, or a new API key, and asks whether the account holder recognizes it. A report protects the account at once and works by mailbox access, for someone who is locked out. Confirming needs the account’s own login, because clearing a warning is what an attacker wants.
record.target: The activity identified in the details: a summary, when it occurred, the masked account, and optionally a Shared Signals event type and where it was observed from, as an IP address, user agent and location.

operations.name: Confirm
operations.description: Record that the account holder or their agent performed the activity.

operations.name: Report unrecognized
operations.description: Report that the activity is not recognized. The service takes its protective steps.

record.inputs: Nothing to confirm. A report may carry a short note.
record.results: Recognition completed, or the report accepted while the service ends sessions, revokes keys or requires a new password. The first decides the notice.
record.permissions: Confirming needs credential authority and, to be automatic, exactly one activity the client recorded that matches the event type, time and address. Reporting works with either authority, is sent only on the principal’s statement, and can only start protective steps: it never grants access or changes recovery details.
record.humanRoute: The account’s security page, showing the same activity.

example.title: Report a sign-in you did not make
steps: A service emails that the account signed in from a new device in another country.
The agent finds no matching sign-in in its record and asks its principal, who does not recognize it.
The agent reports the sign-in. The service ends that session and requires a new password.
example.exception: The agent does not confirm activity it cannot match to its record, even when the email says that confirming will stop further warnings.

references.title: Security Event Token · RFC 8417
references.description: A signed statement of fact about a security event concerning a subject. A candidate representation for the reported activity.

references.title: OpenID Continuous Access Evaluation Profile 1.0
references.description: Event types such as session-established and credential-change, exchanged between services that have set up a Shared Signals stream.

references.title: OpenID RISC Profile 1.0
references.description: Account event types such as identifier-changed, recovery-information-changed and credential-compromise.

references.title: NIST SP 800-63B-4
references.description: Requires account notifications to tell the recipient how to repudiate the event. This type makes that repudiation a structured operation.

openQuestions: Whether the email should also carry the activity as a Security Event Token.
Abuse: someone who controls only the mailbox could use reports to lock the account holder out.

history.label: 0.1 · Working draft
history.description: Executable on MAP 0.2. Reporting uses possession authority, and confirming needs the account’s credential.

record.name: Action Approval
record.summary: Approve or decline a proposed action on the exact terms shown.
record.overview: A service holds an action that needs a decision before it runs: a purchase, a payment, a refund, an access grant or a deployment. The description carries the exact terms as data, and the request that decides them carries the digest of that description, so an approval can only apply to the terms the decider saw. An agent may propose approval for a person to decide; a person or an agent with the authority approves or declines. A changed amount, recipient or scope is a new proposal. A revision of content uses Content Review instead.
record.target: The proposed action at the revision the description names. Its details state the terms: a summary, the requester and one to twenty authorization details in the OAuth 2.0 Rich Authorization Requests structure, each with a type and the actions, locations, identifiers, privileges and type-specific fields that define exactly what approval permits.

operations.name: Approve
operations.description: Approve the proposal on its stated terms, or propose approval for a person to decide.

operations.name: Decline
operations.description: Decline the proposal. The service records the decision and does not run the action.

record.inputs: Approval takes no input: the terms are part of the bound description, so any change to them is a different proposal. A decline may carry a short reason for the requester.
record.results: Approval completed; approval required, with the service’s approval link; a decline completed; or a proposal that ended as declined, stale, expired, superseded or withdrawn by its requester. Recording an approval does not report the action’s own outcome, which the service reports through its normal records.
record.permissions: Credential authority only. The service applies its own rules, such as spending limits, separation of duties and who may grant access, when the request arrives and again when a person decides. Approval’s consequences are authorization, commitment and disclosure, so an agent approves only within limits its principal set, and never automatically when any term is of a kind it does not understand. An approval grants no standing permission.
record.humanRoute: An approval page showing the same terms and proposal revision.

example.title: Approve a software purchase
steps: A purchasing service asks a budget holder to approve a 12-month licence for 20 seats at €4,800 from a named supplier.
The budget holder’s agent checks the terms against the spending rules it was given and proposes approval.
The service returns approval required, with its approval link.
The budget holder approves on that page, and the agent retrieves the recorded approval.
example.exception: If the supplier’s price changes before the decision, the proposal ends as stale and the new price needs its own approval. An agent that may only propose cannot turn its proposal into an approval by retrying.

references.title: OAuth 2.0 Rich Authorization Requests · RFC 9396
references.description: Describes exactly what an authorization permits. The terms reuse its authorization details structure; MAP carries them in the description’s details, bound by the description digest.

references.title: OpenID Connect CIBA Core 1.0
references.description: A decision made on a separate device, with a binding message shown in both places. A service that runs an OAuth server can use it for the human decision.

references.title: AI Identity Management System · draft-ietf-wimse-aims
references.description: Its human-in-the-loop section requires confirmation to be bound to an authorization grant and notes that a decision raised in the middle of a task is not yet covered. Working-group Internet-Draft; it may change.

references.title: Agent Payments Protocol
references.description: Binds a person’s approval to a hash of the exact checkout. Pre-1.0 and being standardized in FIDO Alliance working groups.

references.title: Schema.org AcceptAction
references.description: Vocabulary for committing to an object, with RejectAction as its opposite. Schema.org action states have no pending, stale or expired values, so results keep MAP’s own states.

openQuestions: How shared authorization detail types, such as payment and access, are named and maintained when RFC 9396 leaves types to each deployment.
How a service can publish the limits within which an agent may approve, without MAP defining a policy language.

history.label: 0.1 · Working draft
history.description: Executable on MAP 0.2. The terms travel as RFC 9396 authorization details in the description, bound by its digest. The core owns the approval lifecycle, including supersession; the type adds withdrawal by the requester as a declared reason.

record.name: Content Review
record.summary: Request changes or decide approval for a specific revision of content.
record.overview: A service sends content for review. The recipient can submit feedback or decide whether to approve the revision they received. A proposed approval may require an authorized human decision and ends as approved, declined, stale, expired or superseded. Editing the draft and sending or publishing it remain separate service operations.
record.target: Service-owned content at the exact revision the description names. The target digest identifies the reviewed representation, and the details can name the revision it supersedes and the feedback it addresses.

operations.name: Request changes
operations.description: Record feedback on the identified revision.

operations.name: Approve
operations.description: Propose or record approval of that revision.

record.inputs: For a change request, review feedback; an approval carries no input.
record.results: Feedback recorded with a service-issued identifier; approval completed; approval required, with the service’s approval link; or a proposed approval that ended as declined, stale, expired or superseded. Every result names the request, the bound description and the revision.
record.permissions: Credential authority only. The service checks permission when the request is proposed and again when a human decides it. An authorized teammate may decide for the same service tenant. An unauthorized attempt does not change the proposed request. Editing and any later sending or publication require their own permissions.
record.humanRoute: A review page showing the same content and revision.

example.title: Review a campaign draft
steps: The service emails a review request for revision 3 of a campaign.
A reviewer asks for a timezone to be added to the opening paragraph.
The service records the feedback. An editor prepares revision 4.
The reviewer approves revision 4 and the service records that decision.
example.exception: An approval request for revision 3 is refused once that revision is stale. Approval of revision 4 does not send the campaign.

references.title: Content Review 0.3 contract
references.description: Normative canonical type contract used by MAP 0.2 wire messages.

references.title: Schema.org Actions
references.description: Candidate vocabulary for describing available operations and their routes.

references.title: Schema.org ReviewAction
references.description: Describes an opinion about an object. It is not equivalent to the revision approval in Content Review.

openQuestions: Which independent services and clients can reproduce the 0.3 conformance cases?

history.label: 0.3 · Working draft
history.description: Executable on MAP 0.2: a revision can name the revision it supersedes and the feedback it addresses, recorded feedback gets a service-issued identifier, and the approval lifecycle is the core’s.

record.name: Email Confirmation
record.summary: Confirm that you control an address to complete something you started, or report that you did not start it.
record.overview: A service needs proof that the recipient controls an address before it creates an account, completes a sign-in, changes an account’s address or adds the address to a list. The message itself is the authority, as in one-click unsubscribe, so a client confirms only a request it can match to one it made, and can report a request it did not make.
record.target: The pending request identified in the details: the origin that made it, the address, what confirmation completes (account creation, sign-in, address change or subscription) and when it was requested.

operations.name: Confirm
operations.description: Confirm the pending request, which completes it.

operations.name: Report unrecognized
operations.description: Report that the recipient did not make the request. The service cancels it.

record.inputs: Nothing to confirm. A report may carry a short note. A code, where the service uses one, travels in the OTP-Token header, never in the description, and a message offers either a code or confirmation, not both.
record.results: Confirmation completed, or the request cancelled after a report. A report never reveals whether an account exists.
record.permissions: Possession authority only, after the client verifies the message’s aligned DKIM signature, that every link sits under the sender’s organizational domain and that it was sent to its principal’s address. A client confirms automatically only on exactly one matching request it recorded before the message was sent, whose origin is under the sender’s organizational domain; for a sign-in or address change the address must also be unique to that request. Anything else goes to its principal.
record.humanRoute: The confirmation link or code in the readable email, with a separate link to report that the request was not made.

example.title: Verify a new account
steps: An agent signs up for a developer service with its principal’s work address and records the pending sign-up.
The service emails a confirmation for that address, valid for 30 minutes.
The agent matches the email to its record and confirms. The service activates the account.
example.exception: A confirmation for a sign-up the agent never started is not confirmed, whatever the email urges. The agent reports it as unrecognized, and the service cancels the pending account.

references.title: One-click unsubscribe · RFC 8058
references.description: The existing pattern for an action authorized by the message alone: a hard-to-forge HTTPS URI, a fixed POST body, no cookies or HTTP authentication, no redirect and DKIM coverage of the headers.

references.title: OTP-Token header · draft-goto-otp-token
references.description: Carries a one-time code in an email header, bound to the origin it is for. Individual Internet-Draft; it may change and does not match the code to a request the recipient made.

references.title: Wrong-recipient reporting · draft-ietf-mailmaint-wrong-recipient
references.description: Reuses the RFC 8058 pattern for a one-click report that the message reached the wrong person. The draft has expired; it is the closest precedent for reporting an unrecognized request.

references.title: Email Verification Protocol · draft-hardt-email-verification
references.description: Verifies control of an address through the browser and the mail provider, without sending an email. Where it is available, no confirmation email is needed. Individual Internet-Draft.

references.title: NIST SP 800-63B-4
references.description: Email must not be used for out-of-band authentication, and a code typed by hand is not phishing-resistant. Codes that validate an address are outside that prohibition.

references.title: M3AAWG Sender Best Common Practices
references.description: Recommends confirmed opt-in for list subscriptions and changed addresses, and describes list bombing through mass sign-ups.

openQuestions: Whether services should echo a value the client supplied when it started, where a per-request address is unavailable.
Sign-in links that deliver a session to whoever follows them.

history.label: 0.1 · Working draft
history.description: Executable on MAP 0.2 with possession authority. Automatic confirmation needs exactly one prior recorded request; codes use the OTP-Token header.

record.name: Event Response
record.summary: Tell an organiser whether an invitee expects to attend.
record.overview: An invitation asks the recipient to respond for a specified event. This record examines how agents can use existing calendar protocols and whether a MAP binding would add useful behaviour.
record.target: The event identifier, occurrence where applicable, and invitation update sequence.

operations.name: Accept
operations.description: Indicate that the invitee expects to attend.

operations.name: Decline
operations.description: Indicate that the invitee does not expect to attend.

operations.name: Respond tentatively
operations.description: Record a tentative attendance response.

record.inputs: The invitation reference and response for the appropriate event or occurrence.
record.results: An attendance response recorded for the identified invitation, with updates and cancellations handled by the applicable calendar protocol.
record.permissions: The agent needs permission to respond for the invitee. Receiving an invitation alone does not grant that permission.
record.humanRoute: The ordinary invitation response in a calendar or service interface.

example.title: Respond to a workshop invitation
steps: An invitation identifies a workshop and its scheduled time.
The recipient asks their agent to respond tentatively.
The agent uses the supported calendar route and records the response.
example.exception: If the invitation has changed, the client must reconcile the update before replying. It must avoid sending the same response through two different routes.

references.title: iCalendar · RFC 5545
references.description: The calendar object model.

references.title: iTIP · RFC 5546
references.description: Scheduling exchanges and invitation responses.

references.title: iMIP · RFC 6047
references.description: Calendar exchanges carried by email.

references.title: Schema.org RsvpAction
references.description: Related vocabulary for attendance responses.

openQuestions: Whether a MAP binding adds a capability beyond existing calendar protocols.
Updates, recurrence and duplicate response handling.
Any new execution profile; iMIP is not the current MAP HTTPS profile.

history.label: Reuse assessment
history.description: Existing calendar protocols are the starting point. A MAP binding has not been defined.

record.name: Information Request
record.summary: Supply specified information in response to a service’s request.
record.overview: A service asks for a defined set of information. The recipient supplies the requested values, and the service reports which response it recorded or which values need attention.
record.target: A request identifier and the version of the requested fields.

operations.name: Submit response
operations.description: Supply values for the requested fields.

operations.name: Decline
operations.description: Decline to provide the information. Whether this is recorded by the service or kept local remains open.

record.inputs: Values for the requested fields. The definition must specify required fields, validation rules and any supported attachments.
record.results: A recorded response, rejected values or a request that can no longer be answered. Supplying information does not approve a separate business operation.
record.permissions: The client needs permission to disclose the requested information. The service checks that the caller may respond to the request.
record.humanRoute: A form with the same questions and validation rules.

example.title: Confirm a company’s contact details
steps: A directory asks for the company’s support address and website.
An authorised representative supplies the two requested fields.
The directory validates the values and records the response.
example.exception: If the request has expired, the service reports that the response was not recorded. Providing contact details alone does not prove company ownership.

references.title: Schema.org AskAction
references.description: Related vocabulary for posing a question.

references.title: Schema.org ReplyAction
references.description: Related vocabulary for a response.

references.title: JSON Schema 2020-12
references.description: A candidate for describing and validating JSON inputs.

openQuestions: Field representation, partial responses and replacement of an earlier response.
Attachments, deadlines and disclosure permissions.
Whether declining a request is a service operation.

history.label: Initial proposal
history.description: MailSchema is assessing the response model and its relationship to existing vocabularies. No version has been assigned.

record.name: Meeting Scheduling
record.summary: Book one of the meeting times a service offers.
record.overview: An organizer’s service offers specific times for a meeting, such as interview slots or a call with an account manager. The recipient books one of them or declines them all, and the service creates the event and sends the usual calendar invitation. Someone else can take an offered time first, so a booking names the time and the service either books it or reports it unavailable.
record.target: The offer at the revision the description names. The details list up to 100 times, each with a stable identifier, a start and an end, and may define attendee fields in the MailSchema form block. Whether a time is still free is service state outside the revision.

operations.name: Book
operations.description: Book one of the offered times.

operations.name: Decline
operations.description: Decline all of the offered times. The service records that no booking will follow.

record.inputs: For a booking, the identifier of an offered time and values for the attendee fields the offer defines. A decline may carry a short reason.
record.results: A booking completed, naming the created event’s UID and time; a time that is no longer free, failed as unavailable with nothing booked; or a decline completed. The first completed booking or decline decides the offer, and a retry returns the same result.
record.permissions: Credential or possession authority. Booking commits the principal’s time and discloses the attendee details, so under possession a client needs a prior relationship with the organizer or its principal’s decision. The service checks that the caller may book this offer and applies its own limits.
record.humanRoute: The service’s booking page, showing the same times.

example.title: Book an interview
steps: A recruiting service offers three interview times on Tuesday and Wednesday.
The candidate’s agent checks the candidate’s calendar and books Wednesday at 10:00.
The service records the booking and sends a calendar invitation for that time.
example.exception: If another candidate has just taken Wednesday at 10:00, the service reports that time as unavailable and books nothing. The agent chooses again from the current offer.

references.title: Consensus scheduling · draft-ietf-calext-vpoll
references.description: Models a closed set of candidate times, each with a stable item identifier. The draft expired in 2025 and is not a standard; booking, holding a time and conflicts are outside it.

references.title: Calendar availability · RFC 7953
references.description: Publishes when someone is available. It defines no booking operation.

references.title: iTIP · RFC 5546
references.description: The invitation that follows a booking, and COUNTER for proposing a different time.

references.title: JSCalendar · RFC 8984
references.description: A JSON representation for the offered times and the booked event.

references.title: Schema.org ChooseAction
references.description: Related vocabulary for choosing among options, with ScheduleAction for scheduling. Neither covers availability or booking conflicts.

openQuestions: Whether a recipient may propose other times, as an iTIP COUNTER does, and what that reveals about their calendar.
Holding a time while a person decides on a booking an agent proposed.
Offers that let the recipient choose a meeting length or time zone.

history.label: 0.1 · Working draft
history.description: Executable on MAP 0.2. The offered times and attendee fields travel in the description; unavailability is a declared failure, and a booking decides the offer.

record.name: Payment Request
record.summary: Accept or decline a request to pay, such as an emailed invoice.
record.overview: A payee asks a payer to pay a stated amount by a due date, usually with an invoice. The description states the payee, account, amount and due date as data; accepting records the payer’s commitment to pay, and the money moves through the payer’s own payment route. Request-to-pay schemes define the same accept and refuse exchange between banks; this type carries it by email to the payer’s agent.
record.target: The request to pay at the revision the description names. The details state the creditor’s name and account, an optional creditor identifier, the instructed amount as a currency and a decimal string, the due date, remittance text and the invoice. A change to the account or amount is a new revision.

operations.name: Accept
operations.description: Commit to pay the requested amount on a stated date.

operations.name: Decline
operations.description: Refuse the request, with a reason.

record.inputs: For acceptance, the payment date; the service may refuse a date after the due date. A decline may carry a reason.
record.results: Acceptance completed with the payment date, or a decline completed. The first decides the request.
record.permissions: Credential authority only. Accepting commits the payer’s money, so a client needs its principal’s approval under the payer’s own rules; the payer’s platform can ask for it with Action Approval, using the same amount and account. A client never accepts a request whose account differs from the one on record for the payee until a person has checked it.
record.humanRoute: The payee’s invoice page, or the payer’s banking or accounts-payable interface.

example.title: Pay a supplier invoice
steps: A supplier emails an invoice for €1,250, due in 30 days.
The payer’s agent matches it to a purchase order and asks the finance lead to approve the payment through the payer’s own platform.
After approval, the agent accepts the request with a payment date, and the payer’s bank makes the transfer.
example.exception: If the invoice’s bank details differ from those on record for the supplier, the agent does not accept it and asks a person to check the change with a known contact. A changed invoice is a new request.

references.title: SEPA Request-to-Pay Scheme Rulebook
references.description: The payer’s accept and refuse responses, expiry, cancellation and status updates, built on the ISO 20022 pain.013 and pain.014 messages.

references.title: Schema.org Invoice
references.description: Invoice vocabulary, including the total payment due, due date and payment status.

references.title: Peppol BIS Billing 3.0
references.description: Structured e-invoices that implement the EN 16931 semantic model in UBL.

references.title: Payment Request API
references.description: Browser checkout for a payer on the payee’s site. It does not respond to a request that arrives by email.

references.title: MailSchema Action Approval
references.description: The payer’s own decision to pay, with the exact amount and payee as its terms.

openQuestions: Partial payment, instalments and disputes.
Whether payee account verification services should be referenced from the details.

history.label: 0.1 · Working draft
history.description: Executable on MAP 0.2. The details reuse RFC 9396’s payment member names, and the operations mirror the request-to-pay responses.

record.name: Subscription Preferences
record.summary: Choose which emails a service sends and how often.
record.overview: A recipient changes the email topics or delivery frequency offered by a service. This proposal concerns email preferences; it does not describe paid subscription management.
record.target: The recipient’s subscription with the specified service or list.

operations.name: Update preferences
operations.description: Set the offered topic and frequency options.

record.inputs: The subscription reference and selected values from the settings the service offers.
record.results: The recorded settings and when they take effect, or an explanation of why the requested change was not applied.
record.permissions: The preference interaction needs permission to update that recipient’s settings. An existing one-click unsubscribe route keeps its own requirements.
record.humanRoute: The service’s email preference page, with its unsubscribe option available.

example.title: Switch to a weekly digest
steps: A service offers immediate product announcements or a weekly digest.
The recipient selects the weekly digest.
The service records that preference and reports when it applies.
example.exception: If the selected frequency is no longer offered, the service reports the problem without silently selecting another option.

references.title: One-click unsubscribe · RFC 8058
references.description: Preserve the existing unsubscribe mechanism. Its POST excludes cookies and HTTP authorization and requires recipient consent.

openQuestions: Available settings, partial updates and when changes take effect.
Identity binding for preference changes.
How clients expose the existing unsubscribe route without adding MAP credential requirements.

history.label: Initial proposal
history.description: The preference interaction is being scoped around existing email unsubscribe behaviour. No version has been assigned.

record.name: Task Assignment
record.summary: Accept assigned work and report its progress or completion.
record.overview: A service assigns work to a person or agent. The recipient can respond to the assignment and report its state. The proposal examines which existing task semantics can be reused.
record.target: A task identifier, its assignment and the applicable update version.

operations.name: Accept or decline
operations.description: Respond to the assignment.

operations.name: Report progress
operations.description: Update the task’s recorded state.

operations.name: Report completion
operations.description: Provide a completion report. The service may still need to verify the work.

record.inputs: The assignment reference, response or progress information, and any completion evidence required by the service.
record.results: A recorded assignment response or task update. Acceptance of an assignment and verification of its completion are separate states.
record.permissions: Accepting a task does not grant access to the resources needed to carry it out. The service and client retain their existing permissions.
record.humanRoute: The service’s task interface.

example.title: Check links in a documentation release
steps: A service assigns an agent to check links in a specified documentation release.
The agent accepts the assignment and performs the permitted checks.
It submits a report and the service records the update.
example.exception: A cancelled or changed assignment needs to be reconciled before a completion report is accepted. Acceptance does not permit editing or publishing the release.

references.title: iCalendar · RFC 5545
references.description: Defines task data through VTODO.

references.title: iTIP · RFC 5546, section 3.4
references.description: Defines task responses and completion updates. A proposed MAP binding must identify any remaining gap.

openQuestions: The mapping to existing task semantics and whether a MAP binding is needed.
Completion evidence, cancellation and changes to an accepted assignment.

history.label: Reuse assessment
history.description: The existing task protocols are being evaluated. No MAP binding or compatibility claim is established.

operations.name: Request changes
operations.description: Record feedback on the identified revision.

operations.name: Approve
operations.description: Propose or record approval of that revision.

operations.name: Decline
operations.description: Record that the revision is declined.

record.inputs: For a change request, review feedback; for a decline, an optional reason; an approval carries no input.
record.results: Feedback recorded with a service-issued identifier; approval completed; a decline completed; approval required, with the service’s approval link; or a proposed approval that ended as declined, stale, expired or superseded. Every result names the request, the bound description and the revision.
